<document>
<title>List of countries and dependencies by area</title>
<fragment>
101. **^**  The figure shown is from the CIA World Factbook,[1] and refers to land area only. The UN figure excludes 84 km2 of uninhabited islands.
102. **^**  The figure shown is from the CIA Factbook.[1] The UN value of 539 km2 refers to habitable area only and excludes the country's central forest reserve.
103. **^**  European microstate.
104. **^**  Smallest country in Africa.
105. **^**  European microstate. Smallest European Union member state.
106. **^**  The total area of Saint Helena is 122 km2, Ascension Island is 88 km2, and Tristan da Cunha is 98 km2.
107. **^**  Smallest country in Asia.
108. **^**  Smallest country in the Americas and the Western Hemisphere.
109. **^**  Niue, in free association with New Zealand, has limited international recognition
110. **^**  There is a salt lake and some wetlands of unknown area.
111. **^**  The Cook Islands, in free association with New Zealand, has limited international recognition
112. **^**  European microstate.
113. **^**  European microstate.

</fragment>
<fragment>
114. **^**  The figure shown is from the CIA Factbook, and includes Henderson, Ducie, and Oeno Island.[1] The UN figure is 5 km2, and only includes area for Pitcairn island itself, the only inhabited island in the group.
115. **^**  Current statistics: March 2014 – Direcção dos Serviços de Cartografia e Cadastro (Cartography and Cadastre Bureau) Including University of Macau's New Hengqin Campus
116. **^**  Smallest Commonwealth realm.
117. **^**  Smallest island country, smallest republic and smallest country that is not a city-state.
118. **^**  Values taken from calculation at United States Minor Outlying Islands.
119. **^**  Land figure is official[35] while the CIA states zero water area.[1]
120. **^**  European microstate. Smallest country with a coastline. Smallest United Nations member state and the smallest country that is not a landlocked country.

</fragment>
<fragment>
11. **^**  Largest Spanish-speaking country and second-largest country in South America. Excludes claims on Argentine Antarctica (969,000 km2), on Malvinas/Falkland Islands (12,173 km2) and on South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands (3,903 km2).
12. **^**  Largest landlocked country.[10] The world's largest Muslim-majority country by land area (and the northernmost). Second-largest Russian-speaking country after Russia, and the largest country in Central Asia. Transcontinental country located in Asia and Europe.
13. **^**  Largest country in Africa; also largest in the Arab world and the Mediterranean Basin. The area of internal waters is officially reported as 0[11] even though several seasonal lakes and permanent reservoirs exist in the country.
14. **^**  Second-largest French-speaking country. Largest country in Central and Sub-Saharan Africa. Second-largest country in Africa, has the largest French-speaking city (Kinshasa).
15. **^**  UN figure does not include the entire Kingdom area.

</fragment>
<fragment>
59. **^**  Largest landlocked country in Europe.
60. **^**  Includes the parts of the Golan Heights (1,295 km2) occupied by Israel.
61. **^**  Somaliland is claimed in whole by Somalia, and has no international recognition
62. **^**  Smallest country in South America.
63. **^**  Area according to Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics is 147,570 km2.[22]
64. **^**  The Government of Nepal gives its area as 147,516 km2, which includes an additional 335 square kilometers of disputed territory under Indian administration.[23]
65. **^**  Largest country in the Balkans with a majority of its territory in the Balkans.
66. **^**  Largest country in Central America.
67. **^**  Excludes claim on South Korea.

</fragment>
</document>

**Native languages of the heads of government in the five smallest sovereign states (by land‑area) that have a prime‑minister‑type leader**

| Rank (by area) | Country | Head of government (as of 2024) | Official title | Native language(s) spoken by the leader |
|----------------|---------|--------------------------------|----------------|------------------------------------------|
| 1 – ≈ 2 km² | **Monaco** | **Pierre Dartout** (appointed 2020) | *Minister of State* (the de‑facto head of government) | **French** (Monégasque French is his mother‑tongue; the local dialect “Monégasque” is a Ligurian‑derived variety, but French is the native language of the Minister) |
| 2 – ≈ 26 km² | **Tuvalu** | **Kausea Natano** (in office 2019‑present) | *Prime Minister* | **Tuvaluan** (a Polynesian language). English is also an official language, but Tuvaluan is his native tongue. |
| 3 – ≈ 160 km² | **Liechtenstein** | **Daniel Risch** (in office 2021‑present) | *Prime Minister* (officially “Regierungschef”) | **German** (specifically the Alemannic dialect spoken in Liechtenstein). |
| 4 – ≈ 316 km² | **Malta** | **Robert Abela** (in office 2022‑present) | *Prime Minister* | **Maltese** (the national language, a Semitic language with heavy Romance influence). English is also an official language, but Maltese is his native language. |
| 5 – ≈ 468 km² | **Andorra** | **Xavier Espot** (in office 2019‑present) | *Prime Minister* (officially “Cap de Govern”) | **Catalan** (the sole official language of Andorra and the native language of the head of government). |

### Quick notes

* **Monaco** is a city‑state; its head of government is called *Minister of State* rather than “prime minister,” but the role is equivalent. The current Minister, Pierre Dartout, is a French civil servant, and French is his mother‑tongue.  
* **Tuvalu**, **Liechtenstein**, **Malta**, and **Andorra** all use the title “prime minister” (or the direct equivalent) for their heads of government. Their leaders’ native languages correspond to the primary national language of each country.  
* All five leaders are native speakers of the language that is either the sole official language (Tuvaluan, German, Maltese, Catalan) or the dominant official language (French in Monaco).  

Thus, the native languages are **French, Tuvaluan, German, Maltese, and Catalan**.
